What do the long lives, houses and vineyards of Isaiah 65:20-22 mean?
On the covenantal reading, they are pictures of new covenant blessing: long life pictures eternal life, and eating the fruit of the vine pictures sharing in Christ, the true vine.

Isaiah 65:20 says there will be no infant who lives only a few days, nor an old man who does not fill his days. Verses 21-22 say people will build houses and live in them, plant vineyards and eat their fruit, and their days will be like the days of a tree. Under the old covenant's curses, others ate what Israel planted (Deuteronomy 28:30). In the new order, the curse is reversed. On the covenantal reading, long life stands for the eternal life found in Christ. The vineyard points to Jesus, the true vine (John 15:1-5). "The days of a tree" recalls the tree of life (Revelation 22:2). These are covenant blessings in picture language.
Deuteronomy 28:30: a curse of the old covenant — you will plant a vineyard and not use its fruit.
John 15:5: "I am the vine, you are the branches."

Premillennialists read these as literal conditions in Christ's thousand-year reign on earth. Many amillennialists and others read them as poetic pictures of the final new creation, using the best blessings an Israelite could imagine. Few take them as a description of the present church age.
What do the wolf and lamb feeding together mean (Isaiah 65:25)?
On the covenantal reading, they picture former enemies, such as Jews and Gentiles, reconciled in Christ. "Dust shall be the serpent's food" recalls the curse on the serpent in Eden.

Isaiah 65:25 says the wolf and the lamb will feed together, the lion will eat straw like the ox, dust will be the serpent's food, and they will not hurt or destroy in all God's holy mountain. Isaiah 11:6-9 has a similar picture, and ends with the earth full of the knowledge of the Lord. On the covenantal reading, these animals stand for peoples. Jews and Gentiles were enemies, but Christ "made both one" and broke down the wall between them (Ephesians 2:14-16). The serpent eating dust recalls Genesis 3:14. The curse falls on the deceiver, while God's people are safe. The "holy mountain" is Zion, the church (Hebrews 12:22).
Ephesians 2:14-16: Christ made Jew and Gentile one new man, ending the hostility.
Acts 10:11-15: Peter's vision of clean and unclean animals pictured Gentiles accepted by God.

Many interpreters read the animals literally, as real peace in a renewed creation or in the millennium (Romans 8:21). Others accept symbolism but see it as peace in the whole new creation, not only in the church. Most agree the serpent line recalls Genesis 3.
Was "new heavens and new earth" familiar language to first-century Jews?
Yes. It came from Isaiah, and Jewish writings of the time also used it. The covenantal reading says that New Testament writers expected readers to hear it as Isaiah meant it.

Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 gave the phrase. Jewish works before and around Jesus' time echoed it. 1 Enoch 91:16 speaks of the first heaven passing and a new heaven appearing. The Bible itself also uses the idea of a new world or new age for covenant change: Jesus speaks of "the regeneration" (Matthew 19:28), and Paul of a "new creation" (2 Corinthians 5:17; Galatians 6:15). On the covenantal reading, the apostles did not invent new terms. They used words their hearers knew from the Old Testament, where "heaven and earth" could describe God's people. So to understand Revelation 21 and 2 Peter 3, readers must first ask how Isaiah used the phrase.
Matthew 19:28: "in the regeneration (palingenesia), when the Son of Man sits on his glorious throne".
Galatians 6:15: what counts is "a new creation", not circumcision or uncircumcision.

Others agree the language was familiar, but note that Jewish texts such as 1 Enoch and 4 Ezra often expected a real renewal of the world. They argue that first-century hearers would therefore expect a cosmic renewal, with covenant meaning included.
How can "no more death, mourning, crying or pain" (Revelation 21:3-4) be true now?
On the covenantal reading, it describes life in the new covenant, where God dwells with his people and the curse of sin and the law's condemnation are gone, because "the former things have passed".

Revelation 21:3 says God's tabernacle is with people; he will dwell with them, and they will be his people. Verse 4 says he will wipe away every tear, and there will be no more death, sorrow, crying or pain, for the former things have passed away. On the covenantal reading, the "former things" are the old covenant order, with its law of sin and death (Romans 8:2). Under it, people lived in guilt and fear of death (Hebrews 2:15). In Christ, God dwells in his people (2 Corinthians 6:16). Death has lost its sting (1 Corinthians 15:55-57). The tears wiped away are the sorrow of separation from God. Believers still die bodily, but they do not face the "second death" (Revelation 21:8).
Hebrews 2:14-15: Christ freed those who lived all their lives in slavery to the fear of death.
2 Corinthians 6:16: "I will dwell in them and walk among them" — Paul applies the promise to the church now.

Most Christians read Revelation 21:4 as the future state after the resurrection, when physical death itself is destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26, 54). They note that believers still mourn and die today, so they see the promise as future, with a foretaste now.
What does "Behold, I make all things new" mean (Revelation 21:5-7)?
On the covenantal reading, Christ's new covenant work: a new people, new birth and new life. "It is done" marks the full arrival of that new order once the old had passed.

Revelation 21:5 says the One on the throne declares, "I make all things new." Verse 6 says, "It is done," and he gives the water of life freely to the thirsty. Verse 7 says the one who overcomes will inherit all things and be God's son. Paul uses the same idea: if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old has passed away, the new has come (2 Corinthians 5:17). The verb in Revelation 21:5 is present: "I am making". On the covenantal reading, this is God's ongoing work in Christ. The water of life is offered now: "let the one who is thirsty come" (Revelation 22:17).
2 Corinthians 5:17: "the old things passed away; behold, new things have come."
Revelation 22:17: the Spirit and the bride say "Come", and the water of life is free.

Most interpreters agree the new creation begins in believers now, but say "all things new" points to the whole creation made new at the end (Romans 8:21; Acts 3:21). They see 2 Corinthians 5:17 as the first stage of a cosmic renewal.
How can nations and kings bring their glory into the city if the new creation is after the end of history (Revelation 21:24-26)?
The covenantal reading says this fits the present gospel age: the nations walk in the city's light and their kings bring their glory into the church, while the gates stay open.

Revelation 21:24 says the nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it. Verse 25 says its gates will never be shut. Verse 27 says nothing unclean will enter. Revelation 22:2 says the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations. On the covenantal reading, these details suit the present. There are still nations to heal and kings to bring gifts. There are still unclean people outside (22:15). Isaiah 60:3-11, which John is quoting, pictures nations coming to Zion's light. That is the gospel going out. One covenantal paper sees the "nations" as Gentile believers and the "kings" as Jewish believers, though the text does not split them this way.
Isaiah 60:3, 11: nations come to your light; your gates stay open day and night.
Revelation 22:15: outside are dogs, sorcerers and liars — evil still exists outside the city.

Futurist and amillennial readers say the nations and kings are the redeemed peoples bringing their honour into the eternal city. They read "outside" in 22:15 as the lake of fire, and the healing leaves as lasting life, not ongoing evangelism.
Is the new Jerusalem a physical city?
On the covenantal reading, no. Its gates bear the twelve tribes, its foundations the twelve apostles, and it is shaped like the Most Holy Place. It is the people of God, the bride.

Revelation 21:12-14 gives the city twelve gates with the names of Israel's twelve tribes, and twelve foundations with the names of the twelve apostles. Its length, width and height are equal, 12,000 stadia, about 2,200 km (21:16). It is a cube, like the Most Holy Place in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:20). On the covenantal reading, this is not a building plan. It shows God's people as his dwelling. Paul says believers are built on the foundation of apostles and prophets, with Christ as cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). Hebrews says believers "have come" to the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22). Paul calls "the Jerusalem above" our mother (Galatians 4:26).
1 Kings 6:20: the inner sanctuary was 20 cubits long, wide and high — a cube.
Ephesians 2:20-22: the church is built on the apostles and prophets into a holy temple.

Many futurists read the city as a real place where the saints will live, with symbolic features. Others, such as Robert Gundry, say the city is the people, but the people live in a renewed physical world. Most agree its cube shape points to the Most Holy Place.
What does it mean that the angel promised to show "the bride" and showed a city (Revelation 21:9-10)?
The text treats the bride and the city as one. The covenantal reading concludes that the new Jerusalem, and so the new heavens and earth, are the church, the people married to Christ.

In Revelation 21:9 an angel says to John, "Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb." In verse 10 he shows John the holy city Jerusalem coming down from God. The bride is the city. Revelation 19:7-8 says the bride's fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints, so the bride is a people. Paul pictures the church as Christ's bride (Ephesians 5:25-27; 2 Corinthians 11:2). On the covenantal reading, if the new Jerusalem is the bride, and the bride is the church, then the "new heaven and new earth" John saw with the city is the new covenant people and their life with God. That also shows that "first heaven and earth" was a people and their order.
Revelation 19:8: the fine linen "is the righteousness of saints" (KJV).
Revelation 17-18 shows the other city, Babylon the harlot, also a city that is a woman.

Many readers agree the city pictures the people. But they say a city also implies a place, and the new earth is where the bride lives. They think the new heaven and earth in 21:1 is the setting, and the city in 21:2 is the people within it.
If the Bible is about God redeeming his people, how does recreating a physical universe fit in?

The covenantal reading says it fits poorly. Redemption is about people, so the new heavens and earth are best read as a redeemed people. Others say redeemed people need a renewed world, as bodies need resurrection.

Asked to sum up the Bible in one phrase, many would say "God and the redemption of his people". The covenantal reading asks: how does a remade solar system serve that story? Stars do not sin and are not saved. On this reading, the creation and new creation language is about God making a people for himself. Israel was formed and judged in "heaven and earth" language. The church is the new heaven and earth, where God dwells with his redeemed. Jesus said his kingdom does not come with observable signs, but is "among you" (Luke 17:20-21). The focus is relationship with God through covenant, not the physics of the universe.
Titus 2:14: Christ gave himself to redeem us and purify a people for his own possession.
Luke 17:20-21: the kingdom does not come with signs to be watched; it is in your midst.

Many reply that redemption includes the body. Jesus rose with a physical body (Luke 24:39), and believers will too (Romans 8:23). Since bodies need a world, God renews creation (Romans 8:21; Colossians 1:20). Writers such as N. T. Wright and J. Richard Middleton argue the Bible's story ends with heaven and earth joined, not with escape from matter.
Did older Christian scholars read "the passing of heaven and earth" as the end of the Jewish order?
Yes, some did. John Lightfoot, John Owen and John Brown, all respected Reformed scholars, applied certain "heaven and earth" texts to the fall of Jerusalem and the Mosaic order.

John Lightfoot (1602-1675), a Hebrew scholar at the Westminster Assembly, wrote that "heaven and earth passing" in Matthew 24:35 meant the destruction of Jerusalem and the Jewish state, as if the whole world-frame were dissolved. John Owen (1616-1683) preached that 2 Peter 3:5-7 described the desolation of the Jewish church and state, not the last judgment. John Brown of Edinburgh (1784-1858), on Matthew 5:18, said that a reader familiar with the Old Testament knows the end of the Mosaic economy is spoken of as old heavens and earth removed. On the fulfilled reading, this shows the covenantal reading is not new. Careful scholars long before modern debates saw it.
Lightfoot's Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae (1658-1674) is still used for Jewish background to the Gospels.
Owen's sermon "Providential Changes, an Argument for Universal Holiness" applies 2 Peter 3 to the Jewish state.

Others note that these same scholars still believed in a future bodily return, resurrection and final judgment. Owen and Lightfoot did not apply every "new heavens" text to AD 70. Most historic theologians, including Calvin, read 2 Peter 3 and Revelation 21 as the final renewal.
Is "if the plain sense makes good sense, seek no other sense" a safe rule for reading "heaven and earth"?
The covenantal reading says it is not, if "plain" means plain to a modern reader. Readers must ask what the words meant to the first hearers, who knew prophetic imagery.

David L. Cooper, a dispensational teacher, made famous the rule: when the plain sense makes common sense, seek no other sense. The covenantal reading says this rule can mislead. A modern reader sees "heaven and earth" and thinks of galaxies and the planet from space. A first-century Jew had Isaiah's oracles, the temple, and the Song of Moses in mind. The "plain sense" for him could be covenantal. Jesus' own hearers often missed his figures: they thought "destroy this temple" meant the building (John 2:19-21). Nicodemus took "born again" literally (John 3:4). On the fulfilled reading, the safe rule is to compare Scripture with Scripture and let the Bible's own usage decide.
John 2:19-21: the hearers took "this temple" as Herod's building; Jesus meant his body.
Isaiah 13:10 shows that the "plain sense" for a prophet could be a collapsing sky meaning a fallen empire.

Dispensationalists reply that a literal method means the normal sense in context, including figures of speech. They agree that prophecy uses images, but say figures must be shown by the text. They warn that without this rule, almost any text can be spiritualised.
Is the Bible one story from Genesis to Revelation, with the New Testament picking up where Malachi ended?
Yes, all readings agree. Malachi ends with Elijah coming before the day of the Lord, and the Gospels open with John the Baptist as that Elijah. So the New Testament uses Old Testament language.

Malachi 4:5-6 promises Elijah before the great and dreadful day of the Lord, lest God strike the land with a curse. After about 400 years without a prophet, Mark 1:2-3 opens with "as it is written in the prophets" and introduces John. Jesus said John was the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:13-14). On the fulfilled reading, this matters for heaven and earth. If John is Elijah, then the "great and dreadful day" came soon after him, in that generation. And if the Bible is one story, the New Testament's "heaven and earth" language should be read in the light of the Old Testament, where it often described God's covenant people.
Malachi 4:5: Elijah comes before the great and dreadful day; Matthew 11:14: "this is Elijah who was to come."
Luke 1:17: John goes "in the spirit and power of Elijah" to prepare a people.

All Christian traditions affirm the unity of Scripture. Futurists add that Elijah may come again before the final day (Revelation 11:3-6). Others agree John fulfilled Malachi, but see the great day as including both AD 70 and the last judgment.
What is our authority for this question: church history, the creeds, or Scripture?
All Protestant views say Scripture is the final authority. The covenantal reading admits it differs from many creeds and traditions here, but asks readers to judge by Scripture alone.

The covenantal reading openly says it goes against much church history, the creeds and tradition. It then asks: what is our authority? The Reformers taught that Scripture is the highest judge in all questions of faith. The Westminster Confession says the supreme judge is the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture (1.10). The Bereans tested even Paul's words by the Scriptures (Acts 17:11). On this reading, the creeds are valuable guides, but they can be corrected by the Bible. If Scripture uses "heaven and earth" as covenant language, then believers should follow Scripture even when it changes a long-held view. The writer adds a humble note: he does not claim to have all the answers.
Acts 17:11: the Bereans examined the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so.
Westminster Confession 1.10: the supreme judge of all controversies is the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture.

Others agree Scripture is supreme but say the creeds hold the church's shared reading of it. The Nicene Creed confesses "the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come". They argue that when a reading departs from all historic Christian teaching, the burden of proof is very high.
What kind of book is the Bible: a science book about the universe, or a covenant book about God and people?

The covenantal reading says it is mainly a book of covenant, showing how God relates to mankind. It uses heaven and earth as images of that relationship, without lessening the glory of the physical creation.

The covenantal reading asks: what was God's main purpose in giving Scripture? Is it a science book written to prove that God made the universe? Or is it mainly a covenant book that shows how God relates to his people? It concludes the second. The Bible's own summary of its purpose is about salvation: the Scriptures make one "wise unto salvation" through faith in Christ (2 Timothy 3:15). John wrote "that you may believe" (John 20:31). On this reading, God uses heaven and earth as pictures for his covenant with his people. This does not deny the physical creation's glory. It points to a greater glory: his covenant with mankind and his new creation in Christ.
2 Timothy 3:15: the Scriptures make you "wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus" (KJV).
John 20:31: "these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ" (KJV).

Others agree the Bible is not a science textbook and is centred on covenant. But they say covenant includes creation: God made a covenant with every living creature (Genesis 9:10) and with day and night (Jeremiah 33:25). They think a covenant reading should embrace, not replace, the physical world.
The outer court
The land and the sea: the visible, inhabited world, open to all.

Josephus says Moses divided the tabernacle into three parts. He gave two to the priests as common, open places, and he says they stand for the land and the sea, which all people can reach (Antiquities 3.7.7, sections 181-182). Strictly, Josephus is probably speaking of the three portions of the tent itself (Antiquities 3.6.4 splits it into 20 cubits and 10 cubits). Later readers, ancient and modern, applied the same idea to the outer court. In Solomon's temple the great bronze basin was called "the sea" (1 Kings 7:23-26). In Ezekiel's temple the base of the altar is, in Hebrew, the "bosom of the earth" (Ezekiel 43:14). Scholars such as G. K. Beale and Jon Levenson take the court as the picture of the earth and sea where humanity lives.
The holy place
The visible heavens: sun, moon and stars, the lights God set in the sky.

In the holy place stood the lampstand with seven lamps, the table with twelve loaves and the altar of incense. Josephus says the seven lamps stand for the seven "planets" known in his day, and the twelve loaves for the circle of the zodiac and the twelve months (Jewish War 5.5.5, sections 216-218; compare Antiquities 3.7.7). The curtain at the entrance to Herod's temple was embroidered with a panorama of the heavens, in four colours that stood for the elements (Jewish War 5.5.4, sections 212-214). Philo of Alexandria made similar links (Life of Moses 2.102-105). On this reading, the priests served in a model of the sky, with the lamps as its lights (Genesis 1:14-16 uses "lights" for sun and moon, the same word used of the lampstand's light in Exodus 35:14).
The most holy place
The highest heaven, God's own dwelling and throne, which no human can reach.

Josephus says Moses set apart the third part for God, "because heaven is inaccessible to men" (Antiquities 3.7.7, section 181). In Herod's temple this inner room held nothing at all (Jewish War 5.5.5, section 219). Only the high priest entered, once a year, with blood (Leviticus 16:2, 34). The ark with its cherubim was God's footstool and throne (1 Chronicles 28:2; Psalms 99:1). Hebrews says Christ entered "not into holy places made with hands" but "into heaven itself" (Hebrews 9:24, KJV), so the inner room was a copy of the true heaven. When the curtain tore at Jesus' death (Matthew 27:51), the way into God's presence was opened (Hebrews 10:19-20). In Revelation 21:16 the new Jerusalem is a perfect cube, like the most holy place (1 Kings 6:20).
Formless and empty
without form, and void (tohu wabohu)
I beheld the earth, and, lo, it was without form, and void

This exact pair of Hebrew words appears only here and in Genesis 1:2. Jeremiah sees Judah's coming ruin by Babylon (586 BC) as creation run backwards: no light, no people, no birds, fruitful land turned to wilderness (Jeremiah 4:23-26). Yet God adds, "I will not make a full end" (Jeremiah 4:27). All readers agree this is judgment on the land and people, told in creation words. Isaiah 34:11 also uses tohu and bohu for Edom's ruin.
Hovering over the deep
the Spirit of God moved (hovered) upon the face of the waters
as an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young

The rare verb rachaph (to hover) is used in Genesis 1:2 and Deuteronomy 32:11. One verse earlier God finds Israel in a "waste howling wilderness" (Deuteronomy 32:10), where "waste" is tohu, the word of Genesis 1:2. So Moses tells Israel's rescue as a new creation: God hovers over a formless place and brings out a people. Jesus uses a similar bird picture over Jerusalem just before he announces its desolation (Matthew 23:37-38).
Wind over the waters
the Spirit (ruach) of God moved upon the face of the waters
God made a wind (ruach) to pass over the earth, and the waters asswaged

After the flood, God sends a ruach over the waters, dry land appears and Noah is told to "be fruitful and multiply" (Genesis 9:1), as Adam was. The flood is told as an un-creation and a new start. 2 Peter 3:6 calls it the end of "the world that then was".
Dividing the waters, dry land appearing
let the dry land appear
the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind ... and made the sea dry land

At the Red Sea, a wind divides the waters and dry ground appears, as on day three. Israel walks through as a new people. Isaiah 51:9-10 ties the sea crossing to God's victory over the chaos waters and then speaks of God planting the heavens and founding the earth for Zion (Isaiah 51:16).
Light in the darkness
God divided the light from the darkness
all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings

In the ninth plague Egypt is plunged back into darkness while Israel has light. God again "divides" light from darkness, now between peoples. The prophets use the same pattern: darkness for judgment (Amos 8:9) and light rising on God's people (Isaiah 60:1-2).
Be fruitful and multiply
Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth
the children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied ... and the land was filled

Exodus 1:7 uses the words of the creation blessing for Israel in Egypt. The nation is presented as the carrier of Adam's calling. The promise to Abraham of seed like stars and dust (Genesis 22:17) points the same way.
Sabbath rest
he rested on the seventh day from all his work
There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God

God's rest after creation becomes Israel's Sabbath (Exodus 20:11), then rest in the land (Joshua 21:44), then the temple as God's resting place (Psalms 132:13-14). Hebrews says a deeper rest remains, entered by faith in Christ. Readers differ on whether that rest is mainly present, future, or both.
Finishing the work
the heavens and the earth were finished ... God ended his work
So Moses finished the work

The tabernacle story closes with words that recall the end of creation: the work is finished, Moses sees it and blesses (Exodus 39:43; compare Genesis 1:31; 2:3). Many scholars see the tabernacle as a small creation. This is one basis for reading the sanctuary as a "heaven and earth".
Breath of life
breathed into his nostrils the breath of life
Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain

Ezekiel sees exiled Israel as dry bones. God breathes on them, as on Adam, and they live: the nation is re-created (Ezekiel 37:11-14). Jesus breathes on the disciples and says "Receive the Holy Spirit" (John 20:22), a new-creation act on the first day of the week.
The garden restored
the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden
he will make her wilderness like Eden, and her desert like the garden of the LORD

Return from exile is pictured as Eden regained (also Ezekiel 36:35). Revelation 22:1-2 brings back the river and the tree of life inside the holy city. Readers differ on whether the garden is fulfilled in the church, in a renewed earth, or in both.
Let there be light
Let there be light: and there was light
God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts

Paul says the God who spoke light at creation has now spoken light into believers' hearts through the face of Christ. Conversion is a creation act. This is a clear case where the New Testament uses Genesis 1 for a spiritual reality without denying that Genesis 1 also happened.
A new creation
In the beginning God created
if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature (new creation)

Paul's phrase can be read as "there is a new creation". The old things have passed away and new things have come. Galatians 6:15 says what counts is "a new creation". The covenantal reading sees this as the new heavens and earth already present. The already/not-yet reading agrees it has begun and expects its completion at the resurrection (Romans 8:21-23).
In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth

Most covenant readers accept a real creation here, but note that the Bible opens and closes with 'heaven and earth', so the phrase frames the whole story of God and his people. A minority reads Genesis 1 itself as the forming of a covenant people.
God made the whole universe from nothing. 'Heaven and earth' is a Hebrew way of saying 'everything', as in Exodus 20:11 and Nehemiah 9:6.
Thus the heavens and the earth were finished

'Host' (tsaba) is often an army word, so this reading sees a hint of an ordered people. The finished 'heavens and earth' is also the pattern later used for the tabernacle, which Moses 'finished' in Exodus 40:33.
The six days are complete and the created order is whole. The 'host' are the stars and every creature that fills sky and land.
the generations of the heavens and of the earth
'Generations' (toledot) elsewhere introduces family lines (Genesis 5:1; 25:19; 37:2). This reading says the heavens and earth here open the story of a human family, Adam and his line.
The toledot formula marks a new section. Here it tells what came from the created world, especially the making of man in Genesis 2.
make thy seed as the dust of the earth
God pictures Abraham's family as 'earth'. This is the first clue that earth language can stand for a people in covenant with God.
This is a simile about number only. Abraham's offspring will be beyond counting, like grains of dust; the earth itself is not a symbol here.
Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars
The stars become a picture of Abraham's seed. Together with 'dust of the earth' (13:16), the covenant family is both 'heaven' and 'earth'.
Abraham looks at the real night sky. The comparison promises a vast family; it does not turn the stars into people.
multiply thy seed as the stars of the heaven
Stars of heaven and sand of the shore together describe one covenant family. The oath binds heaven and earth images to Abraham's seed and its blessing to the nations.
Two pictures of a countless number: stars above and sand below. The promise is about growth, not about the meaning of the cosmos.
the sun and the moon and the eleven stars
Jacob reads the dream at once: sun, moon and stars are his household (37:10). Heavenly lights stand for the covenant family and its rulers, a key for Revelation 12:1.
This is a dream with its own interpretation inside the text. It shows that dreams and visions may use stars as symbols, not that ordinary 'heaven and earth' texts are symbols.
I call heaven and earth to witness against you
In ancient treaties the gods were called as witnesses. Moses calls heaven and earth instead, the lasting parties around the covenant, and the warning is loss of the land.
The created world is personified as a lasting witness. It outlives each generation, so it can 'testify' that the terms were given.
I call heaven and earth to record this day
Life and death, blessing and curse are set before Israel with heaven and earth as witnesses. The phrase belongs to the language of covenant law.
Moses appeals to the fixed created order as a solemn witness. The poetry does not deny that he means the real sky and land.
